transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-18
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Carlos Ruiz (Nova VP Eng), Lina Park (Nova Head of AI), Ethan Moore (Cloud Architect)

Summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
Quick scoping to decide POC mode (hosted vs dedicated vs private). Discussed success criteria (latency p95, throughput, cost), workload sizing, benchmarks and timeline. Security/residency requirements flagged. Next steps: pricing, security docs, sample traces, schedule bench.

00:00 - 00:30 Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm jordan from redwood, i'll kick off, maya our se is here as well
00:31 - 01:05 Carlos: thanks, yeah super excited, want to figure out which deployment mode makes sense for our telco use cases - a bunch of real-time customer support and triage, some backend categorization, and internal agent assist stuff
01:06 - 01:45 Maya: great, quick agenda — success criteria, workload sizing (qps, token lengths), benchmarks we'll run, security requirements and timelines. then recommend hosted/dedicated/private for poc.
01:46 - 02:10 Lina: high level success criteria for us: p95 latency under 350ms for 256-token responses for customer chat, reliability 99.9 for peak hours, and cost needs to be under our internal threshold — we can share numbers after
02:11 - 03:00 Ethan: and a hard constraint is data residency — certain subscriber data must remain in our VPC. we need to understand if hosted can meet that or if private is required. also SSO/SAML and audit logs are must-haves.
03:01 - 03:30 Jordan: noted. quick clarifying q: when you say p95 350ms is that including network time to your VPC, or purely infer time once request hits model?
03:31 - 04:15 Lina: we'd like infer time excluding our network, so basically model side p95 under 300ms is ideal. but we can tolerate up to 350ms if it's stable.
04:16 - 05:00 Maya: that's doable depending on model and sequence length. for hosted we usually see p95s in the 150-400ms range for 256 tokens on optimized models with continuous batching offload, but it depends on concurrency and batching policy.
05:01 - 06:00 Carlos: can you clarify the difference again between hosted, dedicated and private from a performance/cost lens? we had a slide earlier but want the quick tradeoffs
06:01 - 08:00 Maya: sure — hosted is our managed multi-tenant API: fastest to start, low initial cost, auto-scaling, but you can't pin physical GPUs; good for early benching. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools (predictable throughput), lower unit cost at scale, and isolation at the tenant level; you get config control over autoscale and burst. Private (VPC or on-prem) is for strict residency/compliance: we deploy a customer-controlled control plane, optional on-prem package; higher setup cost and longer lead time.
08:01 - 09:15 Ethan: about network and VPC — for hosted, can we do a private network path? or is data routed through redwood public endpoints?
09:16 - 10:00 Jordan: hosted uses public endpoints by default. we do TLS in transit and at-rest encryption, and support customer managed keys for some features, but full VPC peering or private-only path is part of Dedicated/Private options. we can do VPC peering for Dedicated and full private control plane for Private.
10:01 - 11:20 Lina: so if we have subscriber data that can't leave our VPC, hosted is probably a non-starter. How much extra time does a Dedicated POC take to stand up?
11:21 - 12:10 Maya: Dedicated can be spun up in ~2-3 weeks for a POC if capacity's available — that's booking, infra prep, and small network setup. Private on-prem takes longer, typically 6-8 weeks including HSM/KMS integration and OLA setup.
12:11 - 13:00 Carlos: ok that's helpful. for the POC we want to validate two things: 1) can you meet our latency/throughput targets with our workloads; 2) verify security controls and auditability. we'll start with a small footprint.
13:01 - 14:30 Jordan: great. can you share the workload profile — avg qps, peak qps, token distribution for prompt+response, and if there are long-run sessions requiring KV cache (stateful chat)?
14:31 - 15:25 Ethan: currently prod traces show avg 12 qps, peak 270 qps during incident windows, avg prompt 40 tokens, avg response 220 tokens. about 20% of traffic is stateful chat needing KV cache and longer context.
15:26 - 16:05 Maya: good detail. for benching we'll replicate that distribution. quick note: continuous batching and prefix/KV caching will help lower latency for repeated contexts; we'll include that in configs.
16:06 - 17:00 Lina: what about model choices — are you running open models or proprietary ones? latency expectation depends on architecture right?
17:01 - 18:30 Maya: yes — we have a curated catalog. for telco real-time chat we often recommend optimized Llama variants or condensed models; hosted supports multiple variants. Dedicated gives you more flexibility to pin a quantized variant and tune kernels. Private allows you to bring your own model binary if needed.
18:31 - 19:30 Carlos: cost — rough ballpark: what does 270 peak qps look like monthly on hosted vs dedicated?
19:31 - 21:00 Jordan: rough numbers — hosted baseline (per-token billing) will be higher per unit at low volume; Dedicated can reduce unit cost significantly once you commit. we'll send a TCO comparison with assumptions. exact numbers depend on token counts, caching hit-rate, and bin-packing.
21:01 - 22:15 Ethan: about benchmarks — what exact tests will you run? will you run from our region and replicate network?
22:16 - 24:00 Maya: plan: 1) baseline hosted tests (3 load levels: avg, peak, stress) using your traces; 2) Dedicated baseline with same load; 3) measure p50/p95/p99 latencies, error rates, and cost per 1M tokens; 4) run failure scenarios (model fallback, region failover). we'll execute from a Redwood test agent in your region where possible and share raw logs and a benchmark spreadsheet.
24:01 - 25:30 Jordan: we'll also run KV cache hit-rate sims and show delta in cost/latency. we'll include guidance for batching policies.
25:31 - 27:00 Lina: security — we need SOC2, ISO certs, KMS integration (customer-managed keys), and audit log retention for 12 months. also RBAC and SAML SSO.
27:01 - 29:00 Maya: we have SOC2 and ISO packages, documented KMS workflows for both Dedicated and Private. Hosted supports encryption at rest and customer-managed keys for specific plans but full KMS/HSM integration and logged key operations are usually part of Private. we'll attach the security pack.
29:01 - 30:30 Carlos: any caveats re: latency when enabling customer-managed keys or VPC peering?
30:31 - 32:00 Maya: minor increases in setup time; runtime latency impact is negligible if network path is direct. the big latency levers are model choice, batching config, and hardware.
32:01 - 33:30 Ethan: for Dedicated, do we get control plane visibility into per-token tracing and cost breakdowns? we need that for chargeback.
33:31 - 34:15 Jordan: yes, Redwood Console provides per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost and latency breakdowns, and tracing hooks. for Dedicated you get deeper retention and access controls.
34:16 - 36:00 Lina: timeline — our internal procurement wants a 6-week POC with clear success gates, and board decision in ~10 weeks. Is that feasible?
36:01 - 37:30 Maya: Dedicated POC in 3-4 weeks is realistic for a minimal footprint if contracts are quick. Private will push to 6-8 weeks. We can stage — start hosted baseline this week, run hosted bench quickly, then spin Dedicated for the deeper test.
37:31 - 39:00 Carlos: staging sounds good. any legal prerequisites to start hosted bench? minimal NDA?
39:01 - 40:00 Jordan: hosted bench can start with a mutual NDA and sample traces; we don't need full contract to run non-prod tests. for Dedicated/Private we'll need procurement paperwork and scoping.
40:01 - 41:30 Ethan: about observability — can you stream logs to our splunk/elk?
41:31 - 42:30 Maya: yes, we support log export hooks, traces, and metrics via pushed endpoints or S3 buckets; for Dedicated/Private you can get full audit log exports.
42:31 - 44:00 Lina: any known limitations with telecom-scale concurrency? e.g., warmup times for KV cache and cold-start behavior
44:01 - 45:15 Maya: cold starts depend on model and sequence length. we recommend warm pools and autoscale configs to reduce cold-starts for spikes. KV cache warm-up is workload-dependent; our bench will include warm-up runs to measure steady-state.
45:16 - 47:00 Carlos: competitors — we've spoken to AWS and Anthropic — what are your differentiators for this POC?
47:01 - 48:30 Jordan: we emphasize production-first ops: transparent perf benchmarks, unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private, cost levers (batching, quantization), and built-in fallbacks so your app doesn't go down if capacity shifts. we'll show concrete numbers in the bench.
48:31 - 50:00 Lina: ok recap then — we'll start with hosted baseline (Jordan to send next steps + NDA), Redwood runs hosted bench using supplied traces, then if results look good we provision a small Dedicated pool and run the full validation including KMS and VPC peering.
50:01 - 51:30 Jordan: yep. i'll send the hosted pricing and sample contract, maya will attach the security pack and benchmark sheet. ethan you'll send traces and network contact. any other questions?
51:31 - 52:00 Carlos: no, that's it. thanks.

Shared artifacts/links referenced:
- Benchmark spreadsheet (mock): https://redwood.example/pocs/nova-benchmarks (shared after call)
- Security pack: https://redwood.example/security-pack (Maya will attach)

Meeting end.
